# Vectors

## Core ideas and reasoning

A vector has magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only. Column vectors describe displacements along perpendicular axes. Add vectors component by component and multiply each component for scalar multiplication. The vector from A to B is position vector B minus position vector A; reversing direction changes its sign. Magnitude in two dimensions is √(x² + y²), from Pythagoras, and in three dimensions is √(x² + y² + z²). A unit vector has magnitude one, found by dividing a nonzero vector by its magnitude. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; a negative multiplier points in the opposite direction. For points on a line, use a starting position plus a scalar multiple of its direction. A midpoint is the average of endpoint position vectors. A point dividing AB internally in ratio m:n is (nA + mB)/(m + n), because it is fraction m/(m+n) of the way from A to B. Sketch arrows to avoid reversing differences. Check endpoint and ratio results against simple coordinate examples.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

Given A = (1, 2) and B = (7, 10), find AB and its magnitude.

AB = (7 - 1, 10 - 2) = (6, 8). |AB| = √(36 + 64) = 10 units. BA = (-6, -8) has the same magnitude.

### Example 2

Find a unit vector in the direction (3, 4).

Magnitude = 5, so the unit vector is (3/5, 4/5). Check √(9/25 + 16/25) = 1.

### Example 3

P divides A(2, 1) to B(8, 7) internally in the ratio AP:PB = 1:2. Find P.

P = A + (1/3)(B - A) = (2, 1) + (2, 2) = (4, 3). AP = (2, 2), PB = (4, 4), verifying 1:2.

### Example 4

Find the magnitude of the vector (3, 2, 2).

Magnitude = √(9 + 4 + 4) = √17 units, approximately 4.12. Its square equals the sum of squared components.
